opus-5.5.text:
I think what draws me to Chinese chess is that it's a game of very concrete calculation, but it also has a strong sense of style and character. Compared with international chess, the board feels more open and the pieces have such distinct personalities: the cannon needs a screen to jump over, the horse can be "hobbled" if something blocks its leg, the elephant can't cross the river, and the generals can't face each other directly. These little rules create a lot of tactical tension. Very often a game turns on one sharp combination, a sacrifice that suddenly opens up the king's position.

When I was a kid, I learned it the way a lot of people in China do, watching older people play on the street, crowded around a stone table with everyone offering opinions. So for me there's also a social and cultural warmth to it. It isn't just a game in a club; it's something woven into everyday life.

And as I got older, I found it a great way to train how I think. You have to look several moves ahead, evaluate positions that are hard to quantify, and accept that your opponent is also reasoning about you. That mix of rigorous calculation and intuition, knowing when to trust a feeling about a position, is something I later found very relevant in research too. So it's both nostalgia and a kind of mental discipline that I still really enjoy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tactical calculation and anticipating an opponent, but it does not connect Chinese chess’s one-on-one format to the player’s personal responsibility for the outcome.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing is that it's complete information. The whole board is right there in front of you. Nothing is hidden, there's no luck, no dice, no cards. If you lose, you lost because you saw less than the other person, or you calculated worse. That kind of honesty is rare. In most of life, outcomes get tangled up with timing and luck and who you know. In xiangqi, it's just you and the position.

The second thing is the river and the palace. People who come from Western chess sometimes think the restrictions are limitations, that the elephant can't cross the river, the advisors are stuck in the palace. But those constraints are what give the game its character. The cannon, for example, is a piece that needs something in between it and its target to capture. So you're constantly thinking about what's in the way, not just what's open. It makes the game feel very dynamic. The opening is fast, the chariots come out early, and you get into fighting positions almost immediately.

And then there's the human side. I grew up watching old men play on the street, on a board drawn on cardboard, with people crowding around and shouting advice. It's not a quiet, library kind of game in China. It's loud and social. Even now, when I study a position alone for hours, I still feel like I'm participating in something that millions of people share. That continuity matters to me.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes the game as having no luck and says a loss comes from seeing less or calculating worse than the other person, linking the head-to-head contest to personal responsibility.

astra-6.text: What appeals to me most is the balance between simple rules and deep strategy. Every move creates possibilities, but it also asks you to give something up. You have to think ahead while staying ready to change your plan. And I enjoy that moment after a game when you look back and realize one quiet move changed everything.
